summary: This repository is a Python-based lunar navigation and landing site analysis platform designed to support safer lunar mission planning. It brings together NASA/JPL scientific datasets, terrain analysis, positioning logic, and visualization tools into a single application for evaluating potential landing sites on the Moon. The project appears focused on geospatial and mission-planning workflows, using Python as the primary implementation language (about 90%) with a smaller HTML component for user-facing interfaces or web-based presentation. In practical terms, it likely helps users assess lunar terrain characteristics, analyze landing conditions, and visualize data relevant to navigation and hazard reduction. The repo’s emphasis on scientific data integration and mission safety makes it a useful tool for research and planning in lunar exploration.
details:
What this is

Lunar Landing Navigator is an educational research prototype for exploring and comparing potential lunar south-pole landing sites and mission dates. It brings terrain, Sun and Earth geometry, and site comparisons into one interactive interface, helping students, researchers, educators, and mission-planning teams make complex lunar data easier to explore. Its intended impact is to support safer, better-informed mission planning and public understanding of lunar exploration—not to certify landing sites or replace professional engineering assessments.

The project’s creative approach is to connect a visual Moon explorer with a scientific analysis pipeline. Users can inspect locations and compare conditions while the application distinguishes real data from illustrative or synthetic inputs, and reports assumptions, limitations, and data provenance rather than presenting estimates as verified NASA results.

Stack

Languages: Python and TypeScript, with HTML and CSS.

Frameworks and software: FastAPI, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js/React Three Fiber, PostgreSQL with PostGIS, and Docker.

Scientific libraries: NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, and PyProj.

Data and services: NASA/JPL Horizons for Sun and Earth positions; NASA GSFC PGDA/LRO LOLA elevation products for terrain analysis; and a NASA Goddard Moon 3D model for visualization.

Hardware: No specialized hardware is required; the application runs on a computer or server. Real-data analysis requires downloaded terrain files, a database connection, and internet access for live Horizons queries.

How it's organized

Text

backend/ FastAPI service, astronomy, and terrain-analysis code

frontend/src/ React and TypeScript interface, components, and API services

db/ PostgreSQL/PostGIS schema, terrain setup, and sample data

scripts/ Terrain-data download, map generation, and validation utilities

data/ Local terrain products and cached data (not committed)

docs/ Architecture, terrain methods, assumptions, and limitations

How it fits together: The interface sends site and analysis requests to the FastAPI backend. Depending on the selected inputs and available files, the backend uses JPL Horizons observations and local LOLA elevation rasters to assess terrain characteristics, landing-footprint hazards, terrain-blocked horizons, sunlight windows, and geometric Earth visibility. It returns results—including scores, uncertainty indicators, warnings, and provenance—for visualization and site comparison. Sample site values and synthetic test inputs are explicitly illustrative; real terrain analysis requires the relevant data products.

The team considered data availability and quality, terrain hazards and landing-footprint constraints, sunlight and Earth visibility, uncertainty, coordinate and scientific assumptions, and the risk of overstating results. The terrain engine and default scoring criteria are a research prototype, not validated NASA standards or a certified landing-safety system.

How to run it

The documented Docker setup uses a Supabase PostgreSQL database with PostGIS enabled and a configured .env file:

sh

docker compose up --build

Then open http://localhost:8000. Downloaded LOLA data can be added for real-terrain analysis; without it, the application labels synthetic terrain rather than presenting it as real data.
